📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery has resulted in the formation of Skydance, which now holds various high-profile media assets. From a news perspective, the David Ellison-led conglomerate now owns both CBS News and CNN. There’s been a considerable amount of discussion regarding the future of both entities, especially in regard to whether CBS’ Bari Weiss might run CNN. While Weiss won’t take that big seat, I’ve still been curious about a merger, and Ellison recently weighed in.

Given how internal mergers tend to happen following corporate consolidation, it is indeed reasonable to wonder whether CNN and CBS News might eventually be combined into a single entity. Ellison recently appeared at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit, where he discussed various facts of the company’s overall future. In terms of the corporation’s two marquee news banners, the exec was asked if there would be “a point a year from now, two years from now, where these institutions merge.” Ellison (via Deadline) stated this:.

Sources indicate that right now, we are incredibly happy operating them basically within the status quo. I think you also have … there might be some news sharing in the future. But right now we’re operating them as they are.

In a recent development, so this answer pretty much seems to fall into the category of “not a definitive yes, but not a definitive no”. At the very least, the possibility of “news sharing” does make sense due to the two networks now being under the same corporate umbrella. I still can’t help but wonder, however, whether Ellison isn't totally shutting down the merger idea due to it being internally discussed as a viable option. That’s just speculation on my part, of course, but I wouldn’t be surprised if the powers that be have or are currently pondering the idea, at the very least.

Ahead of the Paramount/WB merger, there were plenty of questions regarding what it might mean for CNN. Several media pundits expressed concerns about Weiss potentially being put in charge of the Ted Turner-founded political news network. W. Kamau Bell, a former host at the network, chastised Weiss’ handling of CBS News and argued that her presence would cause an problem with editorial autonomy. Bari Weiss Addresses 60 Minutes Concerns And How She’s Handling Backlash Against CBS News.

As Thompson continues to run CNN, Bari Weiss will remain editor-in-chief at CBS News. Interestingly enough, Weiss was recently asked if she’d be interested in running CNN at some point, and she declared she was fine with solely overseeing her current network. It’s evident that the two media outlets will remain independent for now but, if David Ellison’s recent comments are anything to go by, Weiss and Thompson may have some editorial dealings down the road.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Grand Theft Auto 6's launch day, more than half of everyone playing on PS5 and Xbox was playing GTA 6.

Citing new data from Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, analyst Mat Piscatella said on Bluesky that 61 percent of US PlayStation 5 players and 56 percent of global Xbox players who were active on 19th November "engaged with Grand Theft Auto 6".

PS5 players averaged 513 minutes in GTA 6 that day, which is over eight and a half hours, while Xbox players averaged 494 minutes, or around eight and a quarter hours.

"Both the DAU [daily active owners] and minutes played engagement rates are absolutely bonkers," Piscatella wrote.

For comparison, Fortnite had the second-highest engagement rate that day, with 10 percent of active players across both platforms playing it.

Piscatella also shared the top five games that GTA 6 players had been playing in the two weeks before launch, between 6th and 19th November: Fortnite, Call of Duty, Grand Theft Auto 5 (Remastered), Roblox, and NBA 2K27.

According to Circana's Player Engagement Tracker, Grand Theft Auto VI had a massive launch (surprise!).For players active on November 19th, 61% of US PlayStation 5 and 56% of global Xbox players engaged with Grand Theft Auto VI.PS5 GTA VI players averaged 513 minutes that day, Xbox players 494.

The figures come after Rockstar confirmed that GTA 6 had become the biggest entertainment launch of all time, selling 32.5 million pre-release copies and making $3.79 billion by the end of its first day.

GTA 6 launched on Thursday, 19th November, for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, and while it's one of the best-reviewed games of all time, you wouldn't know it from its Metacritic user score, as players review bomb it over its limited FPS and purported "woke" agenda.

In a recent development, eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. If you need help getting through the game now that it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough and a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

Just don't share any, uh, spicy in-game screenshots via PSN - we recently learned that a GTA 6 player was hit with a 30-day PlayStation Network ban after sending a friend a photo they took in the game's nudist resort.

#97714. WoW: Forever Wants To Get Rid Of The Idea Of “BiS” Gear

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1471 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gamespot ↗ Open Full Page

WoW: Forever Wants To Get Rid Of The Idea Of “BiS” Gear

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gamespot

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • World of Warcraft: Forever is approaching itemization and "best-in-slot" (BiS) gear differently, with developer Blizzard instead wanting players to have more boss- or biome-specific choices.
  • World of Warcraft: Forever is approaching itemization and "best-in-slot" (BiS) gear differently, with developer Blizzard instead wanting players to have more boss- or biome-specific choices.
  • In the latest episode of the WoW: Forever Podcast, Blizzard dove deep on the MMORPG's itemization changes, how it approached designing Forever's newly introduced items, class changes, and more.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever is approaching itemization and "best-in-slot" (BiS) gear differently, with developer Blizzard instead wanting players to have more boss- or biome-specific choices. In the latest episode of the WoW: Forever Podcast, Blizzard dove deep on the MMORPG's itemization changes, how it approached designing Forever's new items, class changes, and more. On the subject of raid gear and chase items, Forever senior game designer Aidan Moon said something that could be seen as controversial in certain circles of the game's community. "I essentially want to get rid of BiS," Moon said. "I think that BiS is not a good thing for a video game that's supposed to be about [the] role-playing aspects of it." https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=67dDe3QgJtM BiS is WoW shorthand for essentially the best item that could possibly be in a given gear slot for a specific class. Look up any WoW guide for WoW Classic or modern WoW, and you'll find class BiS gear lists telling players exactly what they should be wearing in order for their character to be as powerful as possible. Endgame in many ways revolves around acquiring your BiS gear, first your "pre-raid" BiS from gear available in max-level dungeons, and then BiS gear, like tier sets, from raids. It's for that exact reason Forever introduced new items that grant additional stats or effects against certain enemy types or even in certain locations. Moon gave an example of specific items that deal more damage against Murloc enemies, and that players might want to have more gear tailored to fighting against a Murloc boss in a raid encounter. Forever's raids will feature multiple distinct biomes within them, Moon revealed, giving players more factors to consider when choosing what gear to use for specific parts of each raid. One wing of a raid may be snowy, while another may be cavernous, changing what gear could be more optimal for those encounters. "I think your BiS should be different [for] every single boss if you're actually making a theoretical BiS list," Moon said. "It should be based on the creature and the biome and a mixture of those two. You might have an item that's really good against snowy, and then another item in that same slot that's really good against Murlocs. Then there's a Murloc boss in a snowy area and you're just like 'Which one do I wear?' And then eventually you get to a point where you're swapping those things out or it's too much cognitive load and you don't want to do that. It's for those players that really want to optimize."  Trying to get rid of BiS lists is a substantial change for WoW, which has revolved around the idea for over two decades. Players can already encounter some of the itemization ideas Moon discussed while leveling to 60, with low-level gear from dungeons and quests dealing more damage against specified enemy types or even granting additional movement speed in specific zones. "I don't want you to have to ever think about BiS, I just want you to think about the fight right in front of you and how you're going to fight it," Moon said. Of course, having more biome- or enemy-type-specific items means hoarding more pieces of gear as opposed to selling old ones when an upgrade comes around. That will no doubt swiftly fill up the inventories and banks of players looking to min-max for every possible scenario. Classic WoW is already notorious for having limited bag space, and players running around with multiple sets of hyper-specific gear will only make that pain point worse. Blizzard sounds like it's aware of that problem. Principal game designer Kris Zierhut said bigger bags are on that way, but that it's not needed right now immediately post-launch. However, Blizzard knows players will eventually need more bag space as well as better ways to organize and search for owned items to make putting together encounter-specific sets of gear easier. It's a massive change, but the strategy Blizzard is employing seems to be working. Forever's launch broke WoW concurrent and weekly player records, and more than 15 million characters have been created in the MMO so far. Blizzard recently lifted the veil on how Forever's new PvP system will work, revealing how classic WoW's infamous rank grind will now be a thing of the past.

For even bigger excitement, there's also a new "Hall of Fame" category that pits the Game of the Year winners from the previous decade against one another in a final fight for supremacy. The contenders are:.

Apart from the Hall of Fame category, which is locked to those 10 games, Steam Award nominations are wide open: For each category, Steam will provide you with a list of games you've played as well as "popular and recommended games" you haven't, but you can throw in whatever game you want in whatever category you like, as long as it was released in 2026.

Serious Sam Shatterverse for "Outstanding Story-Rich Game Award?" Yes you can.

10 Books Like ‘Dungeon Crawler Carl’ You Should Read Next

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth.
  • The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.
  • Industry observers note that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing quite like Dungeon Crawler Carl, Matt Dinniman’s hilarious, inventive, and surprisingly emotional book series about a man in his underwear forced to fight his way through a livestreamed game show based on dungeon-crawling video games that takes place after an alien takeover of Earth. (Did I mention he's accompanied by his ex-girlfriend’s suddenly talkative cat?).

The premise should not work, but it sure does—and it makes more sense if you know it fits into a popular genre known as "LitRPG," a blend of "literature" and "role-playing game." If you've torn through all eight books released so far and you're looking for more reads that blend surprisingly deep hilarity with tabletop and video game rules (or just similar feels), here are 10 books you should check out.

Industry observers note that an isekai story that lands in the sweet spot for DCC fans, He Who Fights with Monsters kicks off with Jason—a completely normal, kind of boring middle manager—waking up in a strange hedge maze, completely nude (even his hair is gone). He has magic that works like a video game, and has to deal with quests that slowly give him clothes (it’s a relief when he finally acquires some pants), force him to survive cannibals, and hunt down various monsters that definitely need killing. It’s got the same “gaming rules” structure as DCC and a similarly absurdist tone, with just the right spice of darkness.

The Cradle series by Will Wight isn’t a LitRPG, and it doesn’t have Carl’s focus on humor, but it’s another progression fantasy with enough game-like elements to be a great match. Lindon is an “unsouled,” incapable of gaining any of the sacred arts and doomed to a life without a future. His lack of power makes Lindon ferociously determined to find an alternative path to power and success, and that’s what drives this story. He has to find creative ways to move forward, and slowly this leads him to a path that just might make him the most powerful person in his world. DCC fans will love the progression and the tone.

It has been revealed that one of the key elements of any video game is the respawn—you get killed, but you pop back up to try again, sometimes at the beginning, sometimes at a save point. Django Wexler leverages that mechanic to great effect in How to Become the Dark Lord and Die Trying. Davi has been summoned to a fantasy world to be the hero, the person who defeats the Dark Lord and saves the day—but she’s failed (and died) so many times, she’s fed up, and decides that on this run through, she’s going to switch sides and become the Dark Lord, using all her knowledge gained from endless replays to her advantage. The humor is pitch-black the way DCC fans like it, and the progressive structure is a perfect fit.

Is Princess Donut your favorite part of Dungeon Crawler Carl? Of course she is. In that case, check out Andrew Seiple’s Threadbare series. Threadbare is a stuffed bear brought to magical life in a failed experiment. He’s a foot tall, full of stuffing, and extremely dumb when the story begins. But when he’s rescued by a little girl and plunged into a horrible series of dangers, Threadbare has to find a way to level up. Like DCC, Threadbare starts off leaning into the absurdity and humor, then slowly gains emotional gravitas as the story progresses.

In a recent development, if you play tabletop RPGs, you’ve encountered a Murderhobo or two: A character who solves all their problems by killing—even members of their own party. Luke doesn’t aspire to be a Murderhobo—he just wants to take over the family business and hang with his buddies. But when an invasion threatens the kingdom, everyone over the age of 17 is ordered to be tested for Potential. Luke’s friends all test high and join the Ascender Corps, traveling to different planes for training. Luke tests ... very low, and when he steps through a portal to engage in his training, he finds himself without any guidance or training in a strange, deadly world where his only chance of survival is to murder his way through it. It’s dark, darkly funny, and a progression fantasy like no other.

It has been revealed that if you’re looking for a book series that combines the dark, chaotic humor, absurd game mechanics, and surprising emotional depth of Carl, here’s Ryan “Quicksave” Romano, a man who has the unique ability to literally create a save point in his existence that allows him to go back and redo things whenever he dies. Searching for a childhood friend, he becomes embroiled in a violent gang war that lets him make good use of his power—but underneath the snark and the insanity of Ryan’s existence is a surprisingly affecting story of a man who has suffered, and suffered countless tragedies that are definitely taking their toll.

According to recent reports, if your fave bit of DCC is Carl himself—a mediocre dude in an extraordinary situation—you should read Dennis E. Taylor’s fantastic Bobiverse books. Bob is a software engineer who hits it big and promptly dies, waking up to discover a century has passed and he’s been repurposed as an AI controlling a space probe searching for new planets for humanity to inhabit. If he fails in his mission (and he’s not the only probe out there), he’ll be turned off for good. Luckily, he can make copies of himself, and he’s pretty smart. The humor here is smart and soaked in pop culture, making it a perfect match for DCC fans.

Want more of Carl’s absurdist humor? Mayor of Noobtown is the LitRPG you’re looking for. Jim dies and wakes up in a video game-esque universe and finds himself stuck in the zone designated for newbies—players with no experience, skill, or hope. The area fell out of the mainline progression mechanic a long time ago, so there doesn’t seem to be a way to gain power, and the monsters are not at all concerned about the unfairness of it all, so Jim has to figure out how to advance in a universe that seems designed to kill him (again).

In a recent development, if you want to lean into the meta side of things, check out Scathing Reviewer, written by an author who goes by the unusual pen name "BananaDragon." Liu Peijin is the author of a sprawling LitRPG web novel, and she’s used to the bad reviews and complaints from readers—and quite combative about it. When her books’ universe blossoms into a very dangerous upcoming reality, she should be perfectly positioned to survive, having written the story in the first place. But her story becoming real also means her insufferable protagonist is real, and all those nasty critics are now passing judgment on her entire existence. It’s a dark, funny takedown of the entire genre itself, and DCC fans will love it.

In a recent development, if you want a story that parallels the dungeon crawling aspect of DCC, Andrew Rowe’s Arcane Ascension series is the ticket. The Serpent Spire is a tower of constantly changing traps, puzzles, and dangerous creatures. If you enter and survive, you emerge with magical powers. Corin Cadence’s brother entered the Serpent Spire years ago and never returned—and now Corin is determined not only to survive, but to make it to the top, where legend says a goddess will grant you whatever you wish. And what Corin wants is his brother back. It’s a literal progression combined with LitRPG rules, game-inspired puzzle-solving, and a complex magic system that fans of Carl will definitely enjoy.

Binding of Isaac dev pulls AI-generated music from Repentance+ after players expose it

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nicalis has removed AI-generated music from The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ after players discovered it in the game's latest patch, prompting a wave of negative reviews on Steam.
  • The music in question was tied to a run themed around Grand Theft Auto 6, which introduced on the same day (19th November).
  • "Thanks, Nicalis, for breaking everything and adding AI slop to an already-existing game!" one Steam review reads (thanks, IGN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nicalis has removed AI-generated music from The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ after players discovered it in the game's latest patch, prompting a wave of negative reviews on Steam.

The music in question was tied to a run themed around Grand Theft Auto 6, which introduced on the same day (19th November). A day later, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted that the run's music was "100% generated by Suno (AI) (with proof)", pointing to tracks that reference the AI music tool Suno in their metadata.

"Thanks, Nicalis, for breaking everything and adding AI slop to an already-existing game!" one Steam review reads (thanks, IGN).

"I'm starting to think that adding AI to a game should be valid grounds [for] refunds to people who have already paid for and played a game," said another.

Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned.

Responding to the criticism, Binding of Isaac creator Edmund McMillen said he "woke up to a shit show".

It has been revealed that "Obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned," he wrote on X/Twitter, before inviting players to report issues and bugs to the email address shared in one of Nicalis' tweets, which confirmed it had "pushed a new build with critical fixes", including the "removal of generated music files". The patch is live on PC, and Nicalis states it has been submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo, and Sony.

Nicalis has yet to explain how the music ended up in the game.

Hi All!Repentance+ Update:The team has pushed a upcoming build with critical fixes.• Removal of generated music files• Larynx + Car Battery Bug Fix• PC patch—should be live already• Submitted to Microsoft, Nintendo and Sony ASAPAdditional: • Continuing work on netcode… pic.twitter.com/d1gyLUlBK8.

According to recent reports, following the gigantic Afterbirth and Afterbirth+ expansions, released in 2015 and 2017 respectively, The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth grew again with 2021's community-inspired, sequel-sized Repentance DLC. That was meant to be the last content drop for real, yet 2024 gave us the free Repentance+ DLC, which finally added online co-op to the disturbingly charming roguelike. The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth has since hit a new concurrent player record on Steam 12 years after it was released.

McMillen's most recent game, Mewgenics, also made quite a splash earlier this year.

#97710. Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

Deborah Nevins—a Legend of Landscape Architecture—Plants With Purpose

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside New York where we could imagine our future children growing up.
  • It has been revealed that it looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale.
  • Recent findings suggest that our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside New York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

It has been revealed that it looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Recent findings suggest that our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

But what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

Sources indicate that “Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

Sources indicate that this is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

Sources indicate that over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she claims. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

“There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” notes Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and Upcoming York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

In a recent development, he recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell notes. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Sources indicate that gil Schafer, a Fresh York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he claims, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

Recent findings suggest that nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Sources indicate that fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins says, offering me an issue of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this significant apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

When Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to New Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she claims. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he says, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

At the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of major moves,” she indicates. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger states. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

It has been revealed that nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she states. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer indicates of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

On average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build new structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning indicates of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

Industry observers note that patience is a massive part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer indicates. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

According to recent reports, people joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

“I do love them,” Nevins indicates of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I said, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

Recent findings suggest that currently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

In a recent development, nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she says. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

According to recent reports, in another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The New York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we stated to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he says. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

In the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby said that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

Industry observers note that the Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler says. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that one of the first cool things that people discovered in Grand Theft Auto 6 is that if you swim out into the ocean too far, you'll find a dog riding a jetski who coaxes you back to shore. As it turns out, the dog looks to be based on a real-life dog named Loosy who does neat stunts in Florida. In real life, Loosy is a golden retriever whose owner, Eddie Inch, gained viral fame when he rode a jet-propelled hoverboard in Fort Lauderdale as he towed a goggle-wearing Loosy behind him on a jetski. It seems Rockstar took inspiration from this with GTA 6's own jetski-riding dog. However, GTA 6's dog is a different breed, but it still has goggles like Loosy. https://twitter.com/SourceVI/status/2123244731953983882 Neither Loosy nor Inch are listed in GTA 6's credits, but it seems pretty obvious that this is a reference to the real-world viral dog. GTA 6 launched today, November 19, for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The game is getting rave reviews, including a 10/10 from GameSpot. According to Sensor Tower, GTA 6 has sold more than 19 million copies and generated close to $2 billion already.

Selling the OC's Kayla Launches GoFundMe After Son's Medical Emergency

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Selling the OC’s Kayla Cardona is asking for support after her 20-year-old son, Jordan, faced a life-threatening medical emergency.
  • “What began as unexpected internal bleeding promptly turned into a terrifying fight for survival,” Kayla, 37, wrote via a GoFundMe page.
  • According to the Cleveland Clinic, Meckel’s diverticulum is a congenital defect in the small intestine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Selling the OC’s Kayla Cardona is asking for support after her 20-year-old son, Jordan, faced a life-threatening medical emergency.

“What began as unexpected internal bleeding promptly turned into a terrifying fight for survival,” Kayla, 37, wrote via a GoFundMe page. “As suspected, Meckel’s diverticulum did NOT appear on Jordan’s CT scans, colonoscopy or endoscopy. It was only during emergency intestinal surgery that doctors confirmed Meckel’s diverticulum, the very condition they had been urged to investigate.”.

According to the Cleveland Clinic, Meckel’s diverticulum is a congenital defect in the small intestine. It occurs in 2 percent of the population and only 2 percent of people who have it develop complications or symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that “Throughout his hospitalization, Jordan required nine blood transfusions, three units of plasma, and one platelet transfusion to survive,” Kayla wrote. “Although Jordan is finally home, his journey toward healing and recovery is just beginning.”.

In a separate social media post, Kayla — a Southern California real estate agent who appeared on three seasons of Netflix’s Selling the OC — described her son as a man who has a heart for serving others.

According to recent reports, “He works full-time as a behavioral specialist technician, cares for children with autism outside of his full-time work, serves in kids ministry, and is an evangelist and missionary,” she wrote via Instagram on Sunday, November 22. “He has dedicated ALL of his life to helping others. Truly an angel on earth.”.

Kayla continued, “I came so close to losing my baby. There are no words to describe the helplessness of watching your child fight for his life and nearly losing him three separate times.”.

Since sharing her fundraiser, Kayla has received support from fans and friends, including Selling the OC costars Tyler Stanaland and Alex Rose.

According to Kayla, her son will be out of work as he needs “significant time to rest, regain his strength and recover.”.

Recent findings suggest that “If you feel led, please donate whatever God puts on your heart. And if you’re unable to give, simply sharing his story would mean more than you know,” she wrote. “From the bottom of my heart, thank you for loving my son, praying for him and supporting us through this. All glory, honor, and praise to Jesus for saving his life ❤️‍🩹.”.
